title: Uniform convergence
objectives: Tell pointwise from uniform convergence, and prove that a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous.

screens.title: Powers on the unit interval
screens.prose: The curve is $f_n(x) = x^n$ on $[0, 1]$, and the band is $0 \pm 0.1$. Raise $n$ and watch a fixed $x$, such as 0.5, and the point $x = 1$.

derive.caption: $n$ = {{n}}: $x^n$ is above 0.1 for every $x$ > {{fixed(pow(0.1, 1 / n), 3)}}, and $1^n = 1$.

screens.question: For each fixed $x \in [0, 1]$, what does $x^n$ tend to as $n \to \infty$?

options.text: 0 for $0 \le x < 1$, and 1 at $x = 1$.
0 for every $x \in [0, 1]$.
options.why: You forgot the end. $1^n = 1$ for every $n$, so the limit at 1 is 1.

options.text: 1 for every $x$, since the curve always reaches 1.
options.why: You watched the right end. At $x = 0.5$, $0.5^n \to 0$.

options.text: No limit near 1, since the curve keeps moving there.
options.why: Each fixed $x < 1$, even 0.99, gives $x^n \to 0$; the moving part only slides right.

feedback.correct: Right. The limit is 0 below 1 and 1 at 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Fix one $x$ at a time and follow $x^n$.

explain.text: Each fixed $x$ gives a sequence $x^n$, with limit 0 if $x < 1$ and 1 if $x = 1$. This is **pointwise** convergence, one $x$ at a time. The limit jumps at 1, though every $x^n$ is continuous.

screens.title: The worst gap
screens.prose: On $[0, 1)$ the limit is 0, so the gap is $|x^n - 0| = x^n$. Raise $n$ again. For each $n$, look at the worst gap over all of $[0, 1)$.

derive.caption: $n$ = {{n}}: at $x$ = {{fixed(pow(0.95, 1 / n), 4)}} the gap $x^n$ is still 0.95.

screens.question: What is $\sup_{0 \le x < 1} |x^n - 0|$, for each $n$?

options.text: 1, for every $n$: $x^n$ gets as close to 1 as we like near $x = 1$.
0, since $x^n \to 0$.
options.why: You took the pointwise limit. For each $n$, $x$ near 1 keeps the gap near 1.

options.text: $\tfrac{1}{2^n}$, the gap at $x = \tfrac12$.
options.why: You fixed $x = \tfrac12$. The sup looks at every $x$ at once, including those near 1.

options.text: $\tfrac1n$, shrinking with $n$.
options.why: You guessed a rate. For $x = 0.95^{1/n}$ the gap is 0.95, whatever $n$ is.

hints.text: The sup over $[0, 1)$ is about $x$ near 1.
So the sup is 1, and it never shrinks.

feedback.correct: Right. The worst gap is 1 for every $n$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Fix $n$ first, then let $x$ run up to 1.

explain.text: For fixed $n$, $x^n \to 1$ as $x \to 1^-$, so the sup of the gap is 1. It does not shrink as $n$ grows. So the curves never fit inside a band $0 \pm 0.1$ on all of $[0, 1)$.

screens.title: Uniform convergence
screens.prose: $f_n \to f$ **uniformly** on $A$ when $$\sup_{x \in A} |f_n(x) - f(x)| \to 0.$$ So for every $\varepsilon > 0$ one $N$ serves every $x$ at once. Pointwise convergence lets $N$ depend on $x$.
screens.question: Which statement says $f_n \to f$ uniformly on $A$?

options.text: For every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $N$ with $|f_n(x) - f(x)| < \varepsilon$ for all $n \ge N$ and all $x \in A$.
For every $\varepsilon > 0$ and every $x \in A$ there is $N$ with $|f_n(x) - f(x)| < \varepsilon$ for all $n \ge N$.
options.why: You let $N$ follow $x$. That is pointwise convergence, which $x^n$ on $[0, 1)$ satisfies.

options.text: There is $x \in A$ and $N$ with $|f_n(x) - f(x)| < \varepsilon$ for all $n \ge N$.
options.why: You checked one point. Uniform convergence controls every $x$ together.

options.text: For every $x \in A$, $f_n(x) \to f(x)$.
options.why: That is the pointwise statement in words. It allows a worst gap of 1 for every $n$.

hints.text: In uniform convergence, $N$ depends on $\varepsilon$ only.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check whether $N$ is chosen before or after $x$.

explain.text: Uniform: $\varepsilon$, then $N$, then every $x$. Pointwise: $\varepsilon$ and $x$, then $N$. For $x^n$ on $[0, 1)$ the $N$ for $x$ grows without bound as $x \to 1$.

screens.title: Stay away from 1
screens.prose: Now use only $[0, 0.9]$. There $x^n$ is largest at $x = 0.9$, so the worst gap is $0.9^n$. Slide $n$ and read the caption.

derive.caption: $n$ = {{n}}: the worst gap on $[0, 0.9]$ is $0.9^n$ = {{fixed(pow(0.9, n), 5)}}.

screens.question: From which $n$ is the worst gap below 0.01?

hints.text: The first whole number above 43.7 is 44.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $0.9^n < 0.01$ for the first whole $n$.

byKey.early: At $n = 43$ the gap is $0.9^{43} \approx 0.01078$, just above 0.01.
byKey.log: You used $\ln 0.1$ in place of $\ln 0.01$. The target is 0.01.
byKey.hundred: 100 works, but much earlier does too. The question asks for the first.

explain.text: $0.9^{43} \approx 0.01078$ and $0.9^{44} \approx 0.00970$, so $N = 44$ works for every $x \in [0, 0.9]$ at once. The sup gap $0.9^n \to 0$. So $x^n \to 0$ uniformly on $[0, 0.9]$, though not on $[0, 1)$.

screens.title: A bump that runs away
screens.prose: Take $f_n(x) = \tfrac{nx}{1 + n^2x^2}$ on $[0, 1]$. At each fixed $x > 0$, $f_n(x) \le \tfrac{1}{nx} \to 0$, and $f_n(0) = 0$. Raise $n$ and watch the peak.

derive.caption: $n$ = {{n}}: the peak is at $x$ = {{fixed(1 / n, 3)}}, height 0.5.

screens.question: What is $\sup_{x \in [0, 1]} |f_n(x) - 0|$ for $n = 10$?

feedback.correct: Right. The peak is $\tfrac12$ for every $n$.

byKey.zero: You took the pointwise limit. For each $n$ the bump still reaches $\tfrac12$.
byKey.tenth: You gave where the peak is, $x = \tfrac{1}{10}$. The question asks for its height.
byKey.edge: You evaluated at $x = 1$: $\tfrac{10}{101}$. The peak is far to the left.

explain.text: $1 + n^2x^2 \ge 2nx$, so $f_n(x) \le \tfrac12$, with equality at $x = \tfrac1n$. The sup gap stays $\tfrac12$ while the bump slides towards 0. Pointwise to 0, but not uniformly.

screens.title: It depends on the set
screens.prose: Take $f_n(x) = \tfrac xn$, which tends to 0 at every $x$. The dashed line marks $x = 1$. Raise $n$ and compare the gap on $[0, 1]$ with the gap further out.

derive.caption: $n$ = {{n}}: the gap is {{fixed(1 / n, 3)}} at $x = 1$ and {{fixed(10 / n, 2)}} at $x = 10$.

screens.question: On which set does $\tfrac xn \to 0$ uniformly?

options.text: On $[0, 1]$, where the sup gap is $\tfrac1n \to 0$; not on $\mathbb{R}$, where it is infinite.
On both $[0, 1]$ and $\mathbb{R}$, since $\tfrac xn \to 0$ everywhere.
options.why: You used pointwise convergence. On $\mathbb{R}$, $x = n$ gives a gap of 1 for every $n$.

options.text: On neither, since the line never lies flat.
options.why: On $[0, 1]$ the whole line sits below $\tfrac1n$, which shrinks to 0.

options.text: On $\mathbb{R}$ only.
options.why: You reversed it. A bigger set has a bigger sup gap, and on $\mathbb{R}$ it is infinite.

hints.text: On $[0, 1]$ the largest gap is at $x = 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the sup gap on each set.

explain.text: On $[0, 1]$ the sup gap is $\tfrac1n \to 0$, so the convergence is uniform. On $\mathbb{R}$ the gap $\tfrac{|x|}{n}$ is unbounded for each $n$. Uniformity is a property of the set as well as the functions.

screens.title: Uniform limits are continuous
screens.prose: Prove: if each $f_n$ is continuous at $a$ and $f_n \to f$ uniformly, then $f$ is continuous at $a$. This is the $\tfrac{\varepsilon}{3}$ argument. One line is flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: Let $\varepsilon > 0$. By uniform convergence, fix $n$ with $|f_n(x) - f(x)| < \tfrac{\varepsilon}{3}$ for every $x$.
$f_n$ is continuous at $a$, so choose $\delta > 0$ with $|x - a| < \delta \Rightarrow |f_n(x) - f_n(a)| < \tfrac{\varepsilon}{3}$.
For $|x - a| < \delta$: $|f(x) - f(a)| \le |f(x) - f_n(x)| + |f_n(x) - f_n(a)| + |f_n(a) - f(a)|$.
Each term is below $\tfrac{\varepsilon}{3}$, so $|f(x) - f(a)| < \varepsilon$. $\blacksquare$
For each $x$, choose $n$ with $|f_n(x) - f(x)| < \tfrac{\varepsilon}{3}$; then choose $\delta$ for that $f_n$.
lines.why: Your $n$ depends on $x$, so the $\delta$ changes with $x$ too. Only uniform convergence lets one $n$ serve every $x$.

hints.text: Fix one $n$ that is close to $f$ everywhere.
Then get $\delta$ from the continuity of that one $f_n$.
Then split $|f(x) - f(a)|$ into three gaps by the triangle inequality.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Fix $n$ first, then $\delta$, then split into three.

byKey.d1: You chose $n$ for each $x$. Then there is no single $f_n$ to give $\delta$.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the flawed line goes to Left out.

explain.text: Two gaps are small by uniform convergence and the middle one by the continuity of $f_n$. Each is below $\tfrac{\varepsilon}{3}$, so the total is below $\varepsilon$. The first and third need the same $n$ at $x$ and at $a$.

screens.title: Why n comes first
screens.prose: In the proof, $n$ was fixed before $\delta$, and the same $n$ was used at every $x$.
screens.question: Why must $n$ be fixed before $\delta$ is chosen?

options.text: $\delta$ comes from the continuity of one function $f_n$. If $n$ moved with $x$, so would $\delta$, and no single window would exist.
The order does not matter; $n$ and $\delta$ are independent.
options.why: You treated them as independent. $\delta$ is read off $f_n$, so it depends on which $n$ was fixed.

options.text: So that $n$ can be as large as we like.
options.why: Size is not the issue. What matters is that one $n$ works for every $x$, which needs uniformity.

options.text: Because pointwise convergence gives $n$ for each $x$.
options.why: That is exactly why pointwise is not enough. An $n$ for each $x$ gives a $\delta$ for each $x$.

hints.text: $\delta$ was chosen for $f_n$ with $n$ already fixed.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Trace where $\delta$ came from.

explain.text: $\delta$ is a property of one continuous function $f_n$. With pointwise convergence, $n$ would depend on $x$, and so would $\delta$. For $x^n$ this is exactly how the proof breaks near 1.

screens.title: The Weierstrass M-test
screens.prose: Take $\sum \tfrac{\sin(kx)}{k^2}$. The curve is the partial sum $S_N$. Each term obeys $\left|\tfrac{\sin(kx)}{k^2}\right| \le \tfrac{1}{k^2}$, for every $x$, and $\sum \tfrac{1}{k^2}$ converges.

derive.caption: $N$ = {{N}}: every later term adds at most $\sum_{k > N} \tfrac{1}{k^2}$, which is below {{fixed(1 / N, 3)}}.

screens.question: What does that give?

options.text: $\sup_x |S - S_N| \le \sum_{k > N} \tfrac{1}{k^2} \to 0$: uniform convergence, so the sum is continuous.
Convergence at each $x$, but nothing uniform.
options.why: You stopped at pointwise. The bound $\tfrac{1}{k^2}$ does not depend on $x$, so the tail bound holds for all $x$ at once.

options.text: Nothing: $\sin(kx)$ changes sign, so comparison fails.
options.why: You forgot the absolute values. Comparison is applied to $\left|\tfrac{\sin(kx)}{k^2}\right| \le \tfrac{1}{k^2}$.

options.text: Uniform convergence, so the sum is differentiable.
options.why: You asked too much. Uniform limits keep continuity; derivatives need more.

hints.text: The bound $\tfrac{1}{k^2}$ is the same for every $x$.
So the tail after $N$ is at most $\sum_{k > N} \tfrac{1}{k^2}$, whatever $x$ is.
That tail tends to 0, and each $S_N$ is continuous.

feedback.correct: Right. An $x$-free bound gives a uniform tail.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Bound the tail $|S(x) - S_N(x)|$ by something without $x$.

explain.text: For every $x$, $|S(x) - S_N(x)| \le \sum_{k > N} \tfrac{1}{k^2} < \tfrac1N$, so the sup gap tends to 0. This is the Weierstrass M-test with $M_k = \tfrac{1}{k^2}$. Each $S_N$ is continuous, so by the theorem the sum is too.

screens.title: Limits of continuous functions
screens.prose: A classmate says: each $x^n$ is continuous, and $x^n$ converges at every point of $[0, 1]$, so the limit is continuous.
screens.question: Is the classmate right?

options.text: No. The limit is 0 on $[0, 1)$ and 1 at $x = 1$, which jumps. The convergence is only pointwise.
Yes: limits of continuous functions are continuous.
options.why: You assumed pointwise is enough. Here the limit jumps at 1; only uniform limits are sure to be continuous.

options.text: The question is empty: $x^n$ has no limit at $x = 1$.
options.why: At $x = 1$, $1^n = 1$ for every $n$, so the limit there is 1.

options.text: Yes, the limit is the constant 0, which is continuous.
options.why: You forgot $x = 1$, where the limit is 1, not 0.

hints.text: Work out the limit at $x = 1$ and at $x < 1$.
Which theorem would make the limit continuous, and does its hypothesis hold?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the limit function, then ask whether it is continuous.

byKey.yes: You took pointwise for uniform. The $\tfrac{\varepsilon}{3}$ proof needs one $n$ for every $x$, which $x^n$ does not allow near 1.

explain.text: The pointwise limit is 0 for $x < 1$ and 1 at $x = 1$: discontinuous. That does not contradict the theorem, because the sup gap stays 1. The theorem needs uniform convergence, and here only pointwise holds.

screens.title: Measuring the gap
screens.prose: Write `sup_gap_bump(n, m)`: the largest value of $\tfrac{nx}{1 + n^2x^2}$ over the $m + 1$ grid points $x = 0, \tfrac1m, \dots, 1$. It estimates the sup gap of the bump from $0$.
screens.question: Complete the function.

widget.starter:
def sup_gap_bump(n, m):
    """Largest value of n*x / (1 + n*n*x*x) over the m + 1 grid points
    x = 0, 1/m, 2/m, ..., 1."""
    ...
widget.solution:
def sup_gap_bump(n, m):
    """Largest value of n*x / (1 + n*n*x*x) over the m + 1 grid points
    x = 0, 1/m, 2/m, ..., 1."""
    best = 0.0
    for k in range(m + 1):
        x = k / m
        best = max(best, n * x / (1 + n * n * x * x))
    return best
widget.how: Check runs 12 hidden tests, each within absolute 1e-9. Five use m = 10000, where 1/n is a grid point and the answer is 0.5. The rest use coarse grids, where the peak at 1/n falls between grid points.

hints.text: Loop $k$ from 0 to $m$ and set $x = k / m$.
Keep the largest value of the formula seen so far.

feedback.correct: Right. The gap stays at $\tfrac12$ for every $n$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Evaluate the formula at every grid point, ends included, and return the largest.

explain.text: With $m = 10000$, each $\tfrac1n$ tested is a grid point, so the code finds $\tfrac12$ exactly. With $n = 3$, $m = 10$ the peak at $\tfrac13$ is missed: the best grid value is $\tfrac{90}{181} \approx 0.49724$, at $x = 0.3$. A grid can only underestimate a sup.

screens.title: Smoothing a digital payoff
screens.prose: A digital option pays £100 if $S > 100$ at expiry. A model smooths the step to $\tfrac{100}{1 + e^{-n(S - 100)}}$. At every $S \ne 100$ the smooth payoff tends to the step as $n$ grows.

derive.caption: $n$ = {{n}}: at $S$ = £{{fixed(100 + 1 / n, 2)}} the error is £{{fixed(100 / (1 + e), 2)}}; the worst error is near £50.

screens.question: With $n = 10$, how far is the smooth payoff from the step at $S = \text{£}100.10$? Give pounds to the penny.

hints.text: The step pays 100, so the error is $100 - 73.11$.

feedback.correct: Right. About £26.89, and the same at $S = 100 + \tfrac1n$ for every $n$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Evaluate the smooth payoff at $S = 100.1$ and subtract it from 100.

byKey.value: You gave the smooth payoff, £73.11. The error is its distance from the step's £100.
byKey.tiny: You assumed the error vanishes for large $n$. Close to the strike it does not.
byKey.half: £50 is the worst error, approached as $S \to 100$. At $S = 100.1$ it is smaller.

explain.text: At $S = 100 + \tfrac1n$ the error is $\tfrac{100}{1 + e} \approx \text{£}26.89$ for every $n$, and near the strike it approaches £50. So the convergence is pointwise, not uniform. A risk check at a few spot levels misses this; hedging needs accuracy near the strike.

ideas: Pointwise: $f_n(x) \to f(x)$ at each $x$, with $N$ allowed to depend on $x$. Uniform: $\sup_x |f_n(x) - f(x)| \to 0$, one $N$ for every $x$.
$x^n$ on $[0, 1)$ has sup gap 1 for every $n$, so it is not uniform; on $[0, 0.9]$ the gap $0.9^n$ is below 0.01 from $n = 44$. The bump $\tfrac{nx}{1 + n^2x^2}$ keeps its peak $\tfrac12$.
A uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous, by $\tfrac{\varepsilon}{3}$ with $n$ fixed before $\delta$. The M-test gives uniform convergence of $\sum \tfrac{\sin(kx)}{k^2}$.

summary.trap: A pointwise limit of continuous functions need not be continuous: $x^n$ tends to 0 on $[0, 1)$ and to 1 at $x = 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use half base times height, with base $\tfrac2n$ and height $n$.

byKey.zero: You integrated the limit. The limit is 0, but each $g_n$ has area 1.

options.text: Yes: the sup gap is $(\tfrac12)^n \to 0$.
No: $x^n$ never converges uniformly, as on $[0, 1)$.

options.text: Only pointwise, since the gap depends on $x$.

options.text: It converges uniformly on $[-1, 1]$, since $\left|\tfrac{x^k}{k^2}\right| \le \tfrac{1}{k^2}$ and $\sum \tfrac{1}{k^2}$ converges.
Only on $(-1, 1)$, since at $x = 1$ the powers do not shrink.
